home.why.display: Most decisions have to be made before the future is revealed.
home.why.lead: Uncertainty is a state of having unknown information about the future. It prevents decision-maker from knowing the consequences of a decision but also comes with great value if managed properly.
home.why.lead-2: EORC uses scenarios to represent the unknown information to identify the hidden value in uncertainty.
home.why.svg.aria-label: Scenario tree: from today, the future branches into four scenarios, while a single forecast follows one straight line.
home.why.h3: Significant value is hidden in uncertainty.
home.why.body: Managing uncertainty via scenario modelling help to make the optimal decision considering the expectation of the unknown future. This helps the decision to be more robust than decision made considering only one future. This also helps to find and quantify the value of flexibility.
home.why.btn: See it in a small example
home.example.eyebrow: What Planning With Uncertainty Looks Like
home.example.title: Managing uncertainty helps us find the value of flexibility.
home.example.head-note: Here is a simple energy storage example showing planning under uncertainty can yield much higher revenue.
home.example.svg.aria-label: Tomorrow's price is either £110 or £10, equally likely.
home.example.figcaption: Tomorrow's energy prices are unknown but we know the distribution of them, 110£/unit or 10£/unit with equal probability.
home.example.li: Whether to charge the battery today at £50.
home.example.li-2: Whether to discharge tomorrow at the unknown price, or wait and discharge the day after at a guaranteed £50.
home.example.svg.aria-label-2: Planning on the average price of £60 squeezes the £110 and £10 outcomes into one number.
home.example.figcaption-2: The average guess squeezes both outcomes into one number.
home.example.body: The average price is £60, only £10 more than the £50 you paid. Storing costs £20, so it looks like a loss.
home.example.answer: Don't charge the battery today at all.
home.example.svg.aria-label-3: Planning for both outcomes: at £110 discharge tomorrow, at £10 keep the energy and discharge for £50.
home.example.figcaption-3: Planning for both outcomes means having an answer for each.
home.example.body-2: If the price is high, sell tomorrow and earn £60 a unit. If it is low, keep it and earn £0. On average that is £30 a unit, more than the £20 storage cost.
home.example.calc: Each case already includes £5,000 to buy the energy and £2,000 to store it.
home.example.takeaway-label: more on average by planning for both outcomes
home.example.takeaway-lead: The average misses the value of adapting.
home.example.takeaway-term: Planning for many possible futures like this is called stochastic optimization.
home.example.flag: Illustrative prices in pounds. Storage starts empty, with no energy losses or extra charges. £1,000 is an average; the low-price case loses £2,000. For simplicity, we omit the fee for the fixed-price sale.
